Lessons.Title: Using Negative Exponents
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: extend exponential equations to negative time inputs, interpret pre-baseline quantities, use reciprocal powers and graph an appropriate window; distinguish negative exponent from a negative output. Original first-party Edulytiks adaptation of This first-party Edulytiks material follows the reviewed local Algebra 1 learning objectives and uses independently authored examples.

Original fictional scale-indicator model P(t)=100·2^t measurement units, with t measured in years relative to a chosen baseline t0. Values: P(−2)=25, P(−1)=50, P(0)=100, P(1)=200,P(2)=400. Negative t refers to previous years, not negative measurement. The model's backward extension is an assumption, not actual observed historical data.
For nonzero b, b^(−n)=1/b^n. Thus 2^(−3)=1/8; 100×2^(−2)=100/4=25. An exponent such as −2 changes the reciprocal multiplier and does not force the entire result to be negative.

Student task: complete a before/after table for a chosen baseline, write a clear context sentence for t=−2, graph points with negative x-axis values, and compare what happens when model factor changes. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for exponent rules, table, correct time interpretation, and responsible graphing-window/domain explanation.

First-party Cool-down (teacher-scored): A model C(t)=64*(1/2)^t begins at t=0. Find C(2) and C(-1), and explain why a negative exponent describes time before the baseline rather than a negative quantity. Numeric responses supported by the mapped exact families may be auto-checked; the teacher scores negative-exponent exact reasoning, pre-baseline context and graphing.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative input time
KeyConcepts.Definition: t<0 identifies time before baseline event, not a negative quantity.
KeyConcepts.Example: t=−2 means two years before chosen observation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exponential graph window
KeyConcepts.Definition: A useful plot window shows both pre- and post-baseline values without clipping.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Consider large growth for positive t.

WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: Each move forward one year doubles output.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Negative exponent means reciprocal, not sign negation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating negative t as impossible without context
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Relative time may legitimately be before an event.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming extrapolated past values are observed
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A model extension is not historical measurement.

SummaryPoints: Negative exponents extend exponential models to inputs before baseline.
Useful graphs include both negative time and positive output.
